comments.text:
People Think Teachers Are Underpaid—Until You Tell Them How Much Teachers Earn By Kaitlin Mulhere.

Bureau of Labor Statistics: 
Because of their SHORTER WORK DAY & SHORTER WORK YEAR, teachers actually earn MORE THAN other educated professionals on an hourly basis.


The average salary for a public school teacher in the United States for the 2023–2024 school year is $71,699, according to the National Education Association (NEA).

Forbes 2024
Average Annual Salary Across the U.S.
Average annual salary nationwide: $59,428.
Average hourly rate nationwide: $28.34.

Before diving into the specifics, let’s look at the big picture: The average annual salary across the U.S. is $59,428. But that’s not the whole story. Shifting our gaze to the hourly perspective, the average hourly rate clocks in at $28.34. These two figures, while distinct, come together to help paint a broader picture of the earnings landscape across the nation.

Andrew G. Biggs & Jason Richwine
No, Teachers Are Not Underpaid: Salaries lag in some states, but nationally, wages & benefits outpace the private sector.

 The average public school teaching position rated an 8.8 on the federal GS scale. After adjustment to reflect the time that teachers work outside the formal school day, the BLS data show that public school teachers on average receive salaries about 8 percent ABOVE similar private- -sector iobs.

It's true that teacher salaries in several states are lagging. Even in these seemingly underpaying states, though, pensions can more than make up the difference. Many teachers also qualify for retiree health coverage, now practically extinct in the private sector.


Using the latest report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ National Occupational Employment Wage Estimates...example, preschool, primary, secondary, and special education teachers earn an average of $54,740 per year. If we drop the preschool teachers, salaries rise even more. Elementary and middle school teachers average $56,420 per year and secondary (high school) teachers earn an average of $58,170. These figures place teachers comfortably above the national average of $46,440 reported by the BLS (link at the top of the list here).

If we compare these salaries to other professions, we find teachers earning a little more or a little less than plumbers and pipefitters ($53,820), chemical plant system operators ($54,690), real estate appraisers and assessors ($57,040), forensic science technicians ($57,340), police officers and sheriff’s deputies ($58,720), and electrical and electronics drafters ($60,350). 

These comparisons do not make teacher pay look too bad. Plus, we should probably factor in something for the fact that teachers do not work year-round.  There is some dispute about how many hours teachers work and what the adjustment should be for the roughly 38 week work-year. If we treat teachers as working three-quarters of the year (39 weeks), then those salaries in the range of $54-58,000 per year would translate to $72,000-$77,000 per year to make them equal on a per hour worked basis.

At that level, teachers would compare to the earnings of network and computer systems administrators ($77,910 per year), nuclear power reactor operators ($78,400), chiropractors ($78,410), and architects ($79,650).  Again, these comparisons do not seem to indicate teachers are underpaid.

An alternative approach would be to see if teachers were in short supply or over-supplied. If teachers are truly underpaid then schools should have a hard time finding enough people to be teachers. If teachers are overpaid, there should be long lines of applicants for open positions. The reality suggests teacher pay is pretty close to an economist’s favorite place: a market equilibrium.

comments.text:
For a single person (young or old), perhaps a widow(er) or somebody with no family ... CDL driving is viable way to earn a living.
For a person with a family, it can more challenging.
For a married couple, both willing and able to enter life on the road, look into it. "Team" Driving can be profitable and rewarding.
For a person who is down on their luck/a day away from the streets, CDL driving can be a lifeline and possibly a new start on life ...

During the first year (typically an Over The Road (OTR) driving job), most can quite literally live out of their company-provided trucks. It's a large closet w/no bathroom, but the mortgage/rent payment is $0 per month. Laundry and biology needs are met at truck stops, gyms and your company's terminal. It's the opposite of a pampered existence, but hardy and/or determined folks CAN hang in there and assimilate to the lifestyle.

Do your research (<read that again) on companies to start with. There are predatory starter companies that should be avoided. There ARE decent ones.
There are predatory "Lease" agreements, where predators paint it as an "Owner/Operator" opportunity, which it IS NOT. Do not get talked into a lease by a starter company.
Be cautious about signing contracts where a starter company offers "FREE!" CDL training. Complete the "contract" year, and you're good. If you quit, you pay, BIG TIME$$$. Research!!!

Get your CDL, your training and your first year of experience, and real pay and a myriad of driving options present themselves, apart from OTR driving jobs.
Get 30 months of experience, keep a clean driving record/no accidents, and you have job options that offer six figures, benefits, PTO, etc.

Just watching the parts of the video about nursing. I was a new graduate nurse recruiter in the Las Vegas area. I covered 4 hospitals in Vegas and 2 in California. One of the hospitals I worked at in Cali was in San Jose. Nurses there made a ton on paper. The cost of living there is insane. That being said...For reference purposes when I posted a position I would have literally 50-100 new grad applicants per position. When we had job fairs at the hospitals we would easily have 100-150 new grad nurses show up. Usually we would have 15-20 jobs total for each hospital. I recruited 20-30 new grad nurses for each hospital about every quarter. Usually I was handling 100-120 new grad nurses resumes per quarter. 

If there are any new graduate nurses on here reading this, some advice from a new grad nurse recruiter from a MAJOR hospital chain...get your foot in the door in whichever department offers you a position. Once you have experience it is way easier to move around- especially at a large hospital. You make connections. You prove yourself. You get to the department you want. There are very few openings in the ER and labor and delivery.
